what_its_for: Sacrosidase is an enzyme replacement medicine used to help your body digest a sugar called sucrose (table sugar). It is used by people who have a rare condition called Congenital Sucrase-Isomaltase Deficiency (CSID), where the body does not make enough of the enzyme needed to break down sucrose. Without this enzyme, eating foods with sucrose or starch can cause stomach pain, bloating, diarrhea, and gas.
how_to_take: Mix your dose of sacrosidase with 2 to 4 ounces (60 to 120 mL) of water, milk, or infant formula. Do NOT mix it with fruit juice, as juice is acidic and will break down the medicine and make it stop working. Take the medicine with each meal or snack that contains sucrose or starch. You may split your dose and take half at the beginning of the meal and half at the end. Never heat the medicine or put it in warm liquids, as heat destroys the enzyme.
dosing: Dosing is based on your weight and age. The typical dose is: Children and adults weighing up to 33 pounds (15 kg): 1 mL (8,500 International Units) per meal or snack. People weighing more than 33 pounds (15 kg): 2 mL (17,000 International Units) per meal or snack. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions, as your dose may be different. Use the measuring dropper that comes with the bottle to measure your dose accurately.
missed_dose: Sacrosidase is only taken with meals, so there is no fixed dosing schedule to miss. If you forget to take it before starting a meal, take it as soon as you remember during the meal. If you have already finished eating, skip that dose and take your next dose with your next meal or snack. Do not double up on doses.
storage: Store sacrosidase in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze it. Keep it in the original bottle and protect it from light. The bottle should be used within 4 weeks of opening, even if there is medicine left over. Write the date you opened the bottle on the label so you can keep track. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not mix sacrosidase with fruit juices such as orange juice, apple juice, or grape juice, as the acid in juice destroys the enzyme and makes it inactive. Avoid adding sacrosidase to hot or warm drinks or foods. Also, work with your doctor and dietitian to follow a low-sucrose, low-starch diet to help manage your symptoms. Avoid foods and drinks high in table sugar (sucrose) unless you take your medicine with them.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, itching, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, wheezing, or a sudden drop in blood pressure. Also contact your doctor if your stomach symptoms (diarrhea, pain, bloating) are not improving with treatment, if your symptoms get worse, or if you have any new or unusual concerns. Let your doctor know if you have a known allergy to yeast or yeast products, as this medicine is made from yeast.
when_it_works: Sacrosidase works right away during the meal when you take it. It helps your body digest sucrose as you eat. Most people notice an improvement in symptoms like diarrhea, bloating, and stomach pain within a short time after starting treatment, especially when following the recommended low-sucrose diet at the same time. It does not build up in your body over time — it works each time you take it with a meal.
special_populations: Children: Sacrosidase is safe and approved for use in children, including infants and toddlers. It can be mixed into infant formula. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: The effects during pregnancy and breastfeeding are not fully known. Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. People with yeast allergies: This medicine is made from baker's yeast. If you are allergic to yeast, tell your doctor before taking this medicine, as you may have an allergic reaction. Diabetics: This medicine may affect how you manage your blood sugar since it changes how your body processes sugars, so discuss this with your doctor.
